name: Krasue
description: A female nocturnal spirit of mainland Southeast Asian folklore, manifesting as a floating disembodied woman's head from which the heart, stomach and other internal organs trail. Belief in the Krasue remains active in rural Thailand, Laos and Cambodia.
full_description: The Krasue (Thai: กระสือ; Khmer: អាប, Ahp; Lao: Kasu) is a female spirit of mainland Southeast Asian folklore. By day she lives as an ordinary woman; at night her head detaches from her body and floats free, the heart, stomach and a length of intestine still attached and dangling beneath. In this form she hunts for blood and raw flesh, often preying on livestock or on pregnant women and newborns, and is associated with luminous lights seen drifting across rice fields. The headless body must be hidden during the night and the head must rejoin it before sunrise; if the body is destroyed or hidden too well, the Krasue will die. Belief in the Krasue remains widespread in rural Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. The figure belongs to a wider Southeast Asian complex of detached-head female spirits that includes the Khmer Ahp, Lao Kasu, Malay Penanggal, Indonesian Kuyang and Balinese Leyak, and Filipino Manananggal.

aliases.name: Ahp
aliases.meaning: from Sanskrit āpyati, 'to cause to suffer'

origin: Belief in the Krasue and its cognates spans mainland Southeast Asia and the Malay Archipelago, with the strongest contemporary tradition in rural Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Closely related figures are reported throughout Malaysia, Indonesia (including Bali), the Philippines and parts of Vietnam.

etymology.origin: Thai กระสือ (krasue). The Khmer cognate Ahp is traditionally derived from Sanskrit आप्यति (āpyati), meaning 'to cause anyone to suffer'.
etymology.meaning: The vernacular Thai name has no fixed lexical meaning beyond identifying the spirit; in usage 'krasue' is now generic for this category of detached-head ghost.
etymology.first_use: Documented in Thai and Khmer folklore long before modern attestation; first systematic English-language description in late 19th- and early 20th-century colonial ethnographies of Southeast Asia.

timeline.event: Krasue/Ahp/Kasu belief established across mainland Southeast Asia as part of folk religion
Thai film 'Krasue Sao' released, establishing Krasue as a mainstay of Thai horror cinema
timeline.significance: Beginning of the modern Thai-cinematic Krasue

timeline.event: Thai film 'Demonic Beauty' (Krasue) released, treating the Krasue legend through a romantic-horror frame
timeline.significance: Mainstream regional revival of the figure

timeline.event: CCTV footage from a lemon-juice factory in Pathum Thani Province, Thailand, was widely reported as depicting a Krasue
timeline.significance: High-profile modern 'sighting' that received national news coverage; an imaging analyst suggested an explanation involving light reflection

timeline.event: Hundreds of teenagers in Ayutthaya Province, Thailand, gathered to watch red lights moving over rice fields, attributed locally to a Krasue
timeline.significance: Crowd-scale modern Krasue panic; landowner attributed the lights to bird-scaring lanterns

timeline.event: Thai romantic-horror film 'Inhuman Kiss' (Sang Krasue) released, gaining international attention as Thailand's submission for the Academy Awards Best International Feature consideration
timeline.significance: Most internationally visible recent Krasue production

cultural_notes: The Krasue is widely understood as a curse on a living woman rather than a free-floating ghost. Protective practices include surrounding sleeping people with thorny branches that the entrails cannot pass; hiding or destroying the headless body during the night; in Cambodia, burying the placenta of a newborn far from the home so an Ahp cannot reach it.
